title: Rereading chapters 9–12
hookLine: reread evil, punishment, old age, self
tomorrow: one verse says love nothing; one says live happily. which is it?

cards: Two texts land a second apart, almost identical, one phrase different. Usually that's a typo, and the second text is the fix. The Dhammapada's chapter on punishment does the same thing with two verses in a row.
Same opening, same ending, one phrase swapped in the middle. On a first read the eye slides right over the second one: didn't I just read this? So which is the fix, and why keep both?

teach.h: TWIN VERSES: FEAR DEATH, LOVE LIFE.

teach.b: Here's the first, in Max Müller's translation: “All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter.”
The second keeps the trembling, keeps the ending, and changes the middle to this: “all men love life.” Read older, the swap stands out. Fear is one way to recognize another person: everyone flinches.
Love of life is the other way: everyone wants another morning. Two doors into the same room, and the room is the phrase they share: you are like unto them. Not some of them.
The verse doesn't sort people into the ones like you and the rest. Now turn a page to the chapter on old age, which explains why a reread can land differently.

teach.h: THE OX GROWS OLD, NOT WISE.
teach.b: “A man who has learnt little, grows old like an ox; his flesh grows, but his knowledge does not grow.” Getting older is guaranteed. Growing isn't.
The chapter on evil adds how growth happens: a water pot fills drop by drop, with harm and, the next verse says, with good.

teach.h: SELF IS THE LORD OF SELF.
teach.b: And the chapter on self gives the job to the only one who can do it: “Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord?”
So older now isn't a number. It's the ox question: did anything grow besides the years? One sign it did: the second twin verse, the one about loving life, no longer slides by.

how: Verses from the Dhammapada's chapter on punishment, with their call to remember that others are like oneself, are among the lines Theravada teachers use when they explain the first precept, not to kill.

o: a second pass through evil, punishment, old age and self
a first look at the chapters on anger and the way
a list of the punishments monks receive for faults

games.q: the reread, chapter by chapter — tap the pairs.
p: grows old; its knowledge doesn't grow

s: the twin verses on punishment are a copying slip, one verse written twice
they differ by a phrase: one says all fear death, the other says all love life. both end: you are like unto them.
the old-age chapter says getting older makes a person wiser
it says someone who learned little grows old like an ox: the flesh grows, the knowledge doesn't.
in the chapter on evil, a water pot fills drop by drop
small harms add up, and so, the next verse says, does good.

games.q: a new guy at work gets teased in the group chat for his accent. you didn't type any of it. what do the twin verses point you toward?
o: he flinches and loves life like you do; say something kind.
you didn't write anything, so it isn't yours to deal with.
wait and see whether he seems to mind before doing anything.
games.why: both verses end the same way: remember that you are like unto them. the teasing lands on someone exactly like you.

practice: Say the two twin verses out loud, slowly, the first with fear death, then the second with love life. Then bring to mind one person who's hard for you right now, and say the middle phrase once more with them in mind: like unto them.
Stay with that person in mind, breathing, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Rereading chapters 9 to 12: evil, punishment, old age and self, read a second time. The repeat that once looked like a slip turns out to be the point.

orig.note: Pali: rod, punishment, violence; the tenth chapter is the Daṇḍavagga, the chapter on punishment.

carryVoice: Your line: older now, and growing, not just aging. Day three of the reread, done.
